doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: Writing out guitar parts and PBG chord sheets
summary: He wrote out rhythm and lick parts for multiple guitars and used piano-bass-guitar sheets to pick up players' ideas.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: “Well can I have a raise on that?” I had a fascinating chat with Bucky Pizzarelli once about, you know all the studio work he did. Because I noticed sometimes there’d be upwards of three or more guitars. And he said the guys sort of had worked out, you know one’s going to do [scats] and one’s going to play big chords and the other is little lines. Did you like to see particular players in the studio that knew that kind of thing?

Here’s what – see because I never did anybody else, I never went to anybody else’s sessions. So as an arranger I had no idea what other guys did. I only knew what they did on the records. So in order to control the speed of how we can get the feel, I started to write the guitar parts out. I would write the rhythms and I would write some of the licks. And I would indicate where I wanted the licks. And then I would write simile. But

basically when I used three guitars or four guitars, I wrote the parts out. Not the little – like I would write the rhythms and I’d indicate when they should play where. And I didn’t realize I did that until I went to California and I came back to New York after about a year and a half later and I did an orchestra date. And one of the guitar players said to the other guitar player, who was like Lou, doing sessions, he said, “See I told you, Calello used to write the parts out.” So, and I heard him say that and what was funny was I didn’t really understand it. Because to me this is the way I worked.
You didn’t know you were doing something that most other people didn’t.

Yeah. But how I learned, in order for me to get the style, what I would do periodically is I would go into the studio for – somebody wanted to record like ten songs and they wanted to do it for a project or something, I wouldn’t write the arrangements, I would go in with chord sheets, which is how we used to make The Four Seasons records quickly. I’d write a – we called them a “PBA” or “PBG” – piano, bass, guitar. And I would write the main figures, the breaks, and they’d know where the cuts were and then we’d give the parts out, “Now you do this and that, and you do this and that.” And then we would talk it out. And what I would do periodically, by doing that and giving it to the musicians, I would hear what the new licks were and what the new styles were that they would put – and I would do that. And then what I’d do is, “Oh they played this but I want that here.” I don’t like – I don’t want them to do this, I want them to do it here. So then I would learn the little things that they would do and figure out where I wanted them in the arrangement.
